overview: The yellow 'TT motor' is the default drive motor in nearly every beginner robot car kit: a small brushed DC motor bolted to a plastic gearbox that trades speed for torque, so the output shaft turns slowly enough to actually move a small chassis instead of just spinning the wheels. It has no positioning feedback and no built-in electronics — it's just two wires, and swapping which wire is positive reverses the direction. It always needs a motor driver (like an L298N or L293D) between it and a microcontroller, since microcontroller pins can't supply the current a motor draws.
simpleSummary: The classic yellow gearbox motor used in nearly every beginner robot car kit.

specifications.shaft: D-shaped output shaft for wheel-hub mounting
specifications.feedback: None (open-loop) unless paired with a separate encoder disc/sensor

pinMap.name: Terminal A
pinMap.function: One motor terminal. Polarity relative to Terminal B determines spin direction.
pinMap.gotcha: Never wire directly to a microcontroller pin — always go through a motor driver; the motor's current draw will damage GPIO pins.

pinMap.name: Terminal B
pinMap.gotcha: Swap A/B to reverse direction — there's no dedicated 'direction' pin, direction is just relative polarity.

useCases.title: 2WD/4WD robot car chassis
useCases.scenario: The default motor for beginner wheeled robots, driven through an L298N or L293D from a microcontroller.

useCases.title: Simple mechanism actuation
useCases.scenario: Drive a small conveyor, rotating platform, or door mechanism where precise positioning isn't required.

oftenConfusedWith: Stepper motors (precise positioning, no feedback needed)
oftenUpgradedTo: NEMA 17 stepper (for precise positioning) or a geared motor with an encoder (for closed-loop speed control)
